headline: Stellwagen's 128-foot edge: haddock on the mud, cod tight to the gravel, tuna working the top
subhead: Bait's stacked from the Bank to Tillies and the bluefin haven't left — steady groundfish and a building tuna bite make for a full-day trip right now.
body_markdown:
128 feet on the sounder, gravel-to-mud transition on the western edge of Stellwagen, and the bottom's showing that broken, patchy return that tells you cod are sitting right on the structure change. That's been my number all week. Not one number for the whole Bank — every drift is its own decision — but that 120-to-135 range on the edge, where the hard gravel gives way to softer mud, has been the most consistent depth for keeper cod since Sunday. Clam bellies and clam/squid combos on a standard cod rig, dropped straight down and worked slow off bottom, six inches at a time. Nothing fancy. The fish are there, they're just not stupid — you jig too aggressive in this clear, settled water and they'll follow the bait up and refuse it.

Haddock have been the better bite, honestly, and they're sitting deeper and softer than the cod — 140 to 165 feet on the mud patches inside Stellwagen Basin and on the flats north of the Basin toward Tillies. Diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, or the two-hook haddock rigs with small hooks and a bit of bait, have been putting good numbers of 20-to-24 inch fish in the box. The mud there is holding worms and small crustaceans and the haddock are working it in loose schools — you mark them on the machine as a low, dense cloud six to ten feet off bottom, and that's when you slow the boat and let people drop. Some boats are limiting on haddock in under two hours of actual fishing when they find the right patch. Other days it's a slower pick, twenty or thirty fish for a full boat over four hours. It's mud fishing — you have to move to find where they're feeding that day, and the areas that produced Tuesday were quiet by Thursday.

Pollock have been mixed in on the deeper gravel edges, especially the drop-offs on the northeast corner of the Bank toward Tillies, 150 to 190 feet. These fish are aggressive — jig fast and vertical with a diamond jig or a heavier jighead and they'll crush it on the drop. Nice fish too, several in the 15-to-20 pound class reported this week, which is a good sign for later in the fall when the bigger pollock stack up on those same edges.

Hake are a night fishery mostly, but for boats willing to make the run and fish after dark, the deep mud in Stellwagen Basin — 200-plus feet — has been holding good numbers. Squid strips or whole small squid on a simple rig, right on bottom, and you can load a cooler with hake in a hurry once the sun's down and they come up off the bottom to feed.

Now the tuna. We flagged this last week — said the bluefin bite would hold as long as bait stayed concentrated on the Bank, and that's exactly what's happened. Mackerel schools are thick over the gravel on the western and southern edges, and the whales are working right through them, which is your best visual marker out there right now. Where you see whale activity and diving birds, push the boat that direction and start looking for surface fish or marking bait balls on the sounder in the upper 40 to 60 feet of water over 100-to-150-foot bottom. Green machines and small green/yellow spreader bars trolled around the edges of the bait have been drawing strikes, and the jig-and-troll guys working butterfly jigs on the fish that show under the birds have had some of the better fish of the season — several bluefin in the 200-to-300 pound class reported off the southwest corner of the Bank and down toward Cape Cod Tails this week. It's not a sure thing every trip — some days the fish are up chasing and eating anything, other days they're finicky under the bait and you need to slow-troll or switch to a smaller profile to get bit. But the ingredients are all there: bait's holding, whales are working it, and water's been clean and settled, not blown out.

Wind's been light out of the southwest most mornings, laying down by midday, which has made for comfortable running to Tillies and back without beating anybody up. That stability is a big part of why the bait's staying put instead of scattering — no big blow to push it off the Bank. If that holds into next week, I'd expect the same general pattern: cod tight to the gravel edges in the 120-135 range, haddock working the mud patches deeper, and the bluefin staying on the bait wherever it concentrates, which right now is mostly the western and southern flanks of Stellwagen.

What I'd watch for is any real wind event out of the east or northeast — that's the kind of blow that can scatter bait fast and push the tuna and the mackerel schools off the Bank structure entirely. Short of that, this is about as reliable a stretch of offshore fishing as we get in early August. If you've got one day to give it, I'd fish the tide change on the gravel for groundfish first thing, then spend the afternoon running the edges looking for whale activity and bait before the light gets flat. That's the program I'd run myself this week.
